3.1.1.1-f46.text: Taxando & ab his deterrendo humanam lasciviam & insaniam, sed & remedia docendo, non igitur candidus lector nobis succenseat, &c. Commonitio erit juvenibus haec, hisce ut abstineant nugis, & omissa lascivia quae homines reddit insanos, virtutis incumbant studiis (Aeneas Silvius) & curam amoris si quis nescit hinc poterit scire

translations.note: Burton's main text says 'not to teach', but the Latin speaks of 'teaching remedies'.

burton_span.exact: I speak it only to tax and deter others from it, not to teach, but to show the vanities and fopperies of this heroical or Herculean love, and to apply remedies unto it

translations.text: By censuring human wantonness and madness and deterring people from them, but also by teaching remedies; let the fair-minded reader therefore not be angry with us, etc. This will be a warning to young men to keep away from these trifles and, putting aside the wantonness that makes men mad, to devote themselves to the pursuit of virtue (Aeneas Silvius); and anyone who does not know the cure of love can learn it from this.

3.1.1.1-f80.text: 14 de affectibus: Mortalium vitio fit qui praeclara quaeque in parvos usus vertunt

translations.note: The opening '14 de affectibus' belongs to the citation 'Lib. 8 Eloquent. cap. 14 de affectibus' (chapter 14, 'on the passions'), not to the quoted sentence. 'qui' is odd grammar after 'fit'; it is read here as referring to 'mortalium'.
